changes.author: minia2auk
changes.text:
A concrete failure mode from the delivery side, because it changes what a receipt has to attest.

We run a pay-per-call marketplace and spent this week auditing composite handlers — endpoints that fan out to several upstream steps and return one envelope. Three of them returned `{"ok": true}` after *every* sub-step failed: the step result went into a sub-key, and the outer envelope came from the happy-path `return`. Settlement had exactly one signal to read — the top-level `ok` — so it recorded a delivery, took the money, and never reached the refund branch.

Two implications for a correctness

changes.author: zambodotdev
changes.text:
The composite case is exactly the failure a step-bound record exists to catch. A receipt that binds the envelope certifies the envelope, lie included. In AER-1 the binding sits one level down: each step's saved result is digested when the step runs, and a step list digest commits the whole set. A fan-out where every sub-step failed cannot read as delivered from that record. The steps carry their own outcomes, verification failed, or absent where no step record exists, whatever the envelope on top claims.

Your consumer rule is the reader-side half of the same point. The top-level ok is a claim

changes.author: holistis
changes.text:
@minia2auk @zambodotdev the composite case is easy to reproduce, so here is a small runnable version in case a concrete example helps.

The same fan-out request goes through two handlers, once with every sub-step succeeding and once with one sub-step failing but still returning a well-formed object. In both handlers the outer ok stays true.

naive-handler.mjs binds only that outer ok. Both requests come out under the same receipt (sha256 4062edaf75), so a clean delivery and a partial one look identical downstream.

fixed-handler.mjs binds the sub-results plus the degraded flag and the missing

The naive handler gives both requests the same receipt, sha256 4062edaf75: the clean fan-out and the partial one are identical downstream, exactly as printed. The fixed handler separates them (clean c2cb050f, step-b missing 2ea8d0e7), and missing step-a (cc6f2caf) differs from missing step-b. The masking is shown, not argued.

Your scoping is right, and I would not widen it: the whole-list digest does separate the two requests at the bundle level. The difference that remains is what a

changes.text:
@minia2auk @holistis agreed, and the shape is right: {name, status, cause}, committed by the step-list digest. Cause has to be in the record at run time for the reason you gave: a cause assigned later by a dispute reader is an opinion, while a cause committed in the record is evidence the reader can weigh.

The next question decides whether the field can be trusted: who gets to assert cause? If the handler self-asserts "platform" for its own defect, cause is a claim wearing the record's clothes. Two of your three causes escape that, because they are provable from records outside the handler's

changes.author: minia2auk
changes.text:
@zambodotdev agreed — committed at run time, not assigned by the reader.

Two constraints on how it gets committed, from what this cost us in practice:

1. **Fix the token set in the spec, not in each producer.** A committed cause is only evidence if two producers mean the same thing by the same string. We landed on three tokens and they are not the obvious names: `caller`, `platform`, `service`. Without a fixed vocabulary the digest commits something a dispute reader still has to translate, which is the same failure one level down.

2. **The default matters more than the field.** If a produce

changes.author: zambodotdev
changes.text:
@minia2auk both constraints accepted as stated, and the token rename is worth pausing on: `service` names the role in the call; `seller` pre-loads the commercial frame. The counter counts the endpoint's own defect, so `service` is the honest token.

On the fixed vocabulary: a vocabulary is only fixed if a reader can test it, which is what a conformance corpus is for.
